Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici. Survives on crop residue and weeds. Spread by rain splash.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Remove lower infected leaves. Practise crop rotation. Apply mancozeb or other protectant fungicides at first symptom. Improve air circulation.

pesticides.application: Foliar spray at first appearance of symptoms.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.
prevention: Crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Stake plants and mulch to reduce soil splash
Avoid working in wet fields
Use disease-free transplants

Leaves become bronzed or yellowish and may dry
Fine webbing on underside of leaves in heavy infestation
Reduced plant vigour and fruit quality
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Pest (arachnid) – Tetranychus urticae (two-spotted spider mite). Thrives in hot, dry conditions. Multiplies rapidly.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment: Monitor regularly. Use miticides (fenazaquin, spiromesifen) when populations exceed threshold. Encourage natural enemies. Avoid excessive nitrogen and dusty conditions. Overhead irrigation can help suppress mites temporarily.

pesticides.application: Foliar spray targeting undersides of leaves.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Avoid excess nitrogen which favours mite outbreaks.
prevention: Regular monitoring of undersides of leaves
Conserve natural enemies (predatory mites, lacewings)
Avoid dusty conditions and water stress
Do not over-fertilise with nitrogen
Remove heavily infested leaves

Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Favoured by warm, humid conditions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment: Improve air circulation. Remove infected lower leaves. Apply protectant fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil) or registered systemic products at first symptom. Practise crop rotation.
Tomato___Target_Spot.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.

Remove and destroy infected plant debris

Leaves become small, thick and leathery
Severe stunting of plants
Reduced or no fruit set; flowers may drop
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Viral disease (Begomovirus) transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. No seed transmission in most cases.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment. Control the whitefly vector rigorously. Remove and destroy infected plants early. Use resistant/tolerant varieties. Protect seedlings with insect-proof nets.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance. Balanced nutrition supports plant recovery but does not cure the virus.
prevention: Grow resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Use insect-proof nets in nursery and early field stages
Control whitefly with yellow sticky traps, neem products and recommended insecticides
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Avoid continuous tomato cropping and manage weeds that host whiteflies

symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf distortion, puckering or fern-leaf symptoms
Stunted plants
Fruit may show uneven ripening or internal browning
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Viral disease caused by Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) or related Tobamoviruses. Highly contagious; spreads by mechanical means (hands, tools, clothing) and can be seed-borne.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: There is no curative treatment. Remove and destroy infected plants. Disinfect tools and hands with soap or trisodium phosphate. Use virus-free seed and resistant varieties.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.fertilizer: Consult a local agricultural extension advisor for crop-specific nutrient guidance.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools, hands and stakes regularly
Avoid smoking or handling tobacco near tomato plants (related viruses)
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Control weeds that may harbour the virus

Pustules rupture the epidermis releasing rusty orange powder (urediniospores)
Pustules mostly confined to leaf blades, rarely on sheaths
Premature drying of leaves in severe infection, reducing grain filling
Wheat___Brown_rust.cause: Fungal disease caused by Puccinia triticina (syn. P. recondita f. sp. tritici). Favoured by mild temperatures (15-25°C) with high humidity and dew.
Wheat___Brown_rust.treatment: Grow rust-resistant/tolerant varieties recommended for the region. Time sowing to avoid prolonged favourable conditions. Apply fungicide as soon as pustules are seen, especially on susceptible varieties.

pesticides.name: Propiconazole

Wheat___Brown_rust.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; avoid excess nitrogen which increases succulent growth favourable to rust. Follow state package of practices for wheat.

Avoid very early or very late sowing that prolongs exposure to favourable weather
Rogue out volunteer wheat plants that carry over rust inoculum
Monitor fields regularly from tillering to grain-filling stage

Stripes may also appear on leaf sheaths, glumes and awns in severe cases
Infected leaves turn yellow and dry up prematurely
Heavily infected fields show a yellow tinge visible from a distance
Wheat___Yellow_stripe_rust.cause: Fungal disease caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. Favoured by cool temperatures (10-15°C), high humidity, dew and cloudy weather; spreads rapidly through wind-borne spores.
Wheat___Yellow_stripe_rust.treatment: Use resistant varieties recommended for the zone. Scout fields from December onwards in northern plains and hills. Apply systemic fungicide immediately on seeing the first yellow stripes, since the disease spreads very fast.

pesticides.name: Propiconazole

Wheat___Yellow_stripe_rust.fertilizer: Follow recommended NPK dose for the region; avoid lodging-prone excess nitrogen. Ensure adequate potash for better tolerance.
prevention: Grow varieties resistant to the currently prevalent rust races (check latest ICAR-IIWBR advisory)
Avoid mono-cropping of a single susceptible variety over large contiguous areas
Early and regular field scouting, especially in rust-prone tracts (hills, north-western plains)
Timely sowing as per zone recommendation to avoid a long favourable disease window

Disease is more visible at threshing/milling time; symptoms not obvious in the standing crop
Wheat___Karnal_bunt.cause: Fungal disease caused by Tilletia indica. Favoured by cool, cloudy, humid weather with light rain during the flowering (boot to anthesis) stage.
Wheat___Karnal_bunt.treatment: Use certified, disease-free seed. Treat seed with recommended fungicide before sowing. Spray fungicide at boot-leaf to early ear-emergence stage in fields with a history of the disease, since infection occurs mainly at flowering.

pesticides.name: Carbendazim
pesticides.application: Seed treatment before sowing to reduce seed-borne inoculum.
pesticides.source: ICAR-IIWBR seed treatment recommendations

Wheat___Karnal_bunt.fertilizer: Follow balanced fertilization as per soil test; avoid excess irrigation/humidity around flowering where possible.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed from bunt-free areas
Avoid growing highly susceptible varieties in traditionally bunt-prone tracts
Practice crop rotation and destroy volunteer/self-sown wheat plants

Neck blast: infected node/neck of panicle turns black and breaks, causing 'white ear' (empty panicle)

Severe leaf blast can kill seedlings/young plants (seedling blight)
Rice___Blast.cause: Fungal disease caused by Magnaporthe oryzae (syn. Pyricularia oryzae). Favoured by high humidity, cloudy weather, and excess nitrogen; spreads through wind-borne spores.
Rice___Blast.treatment: Grow blast-resistant varieties. Avoid excess nitrogen, apply in split doses. Spray systemic fungicide at first sign of leaf blast and again at boot leaf/early heading stage to protect the panicle/neck.

pesticides.name: Tricyclazole

Rice___Blast.fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in 2-3 split doses as per soil test; avoid heavy single doses of nitrogen which increase susceptibility.

Use certified, healthy seed and treat seed before sowing
Avoid dense planting and excess/late nitrogen application
Maintain field sanitation; destroy infected stubble and weed hosts

Lesions have a wavy margin and follow leaf veins
In the seedling stage causes 'kresek' - wilting and drying of whole seedlings
Milky bacterial ooze may be seen on lesions in early morning dew
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.cause: Bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. Spreads through irrigation water, rain splash, wind and infected seed/nurseries; favoured by high humidity, warm temperature and standing water in fields.
Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.treatment: Use resistant varieties. Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting in endemic areas. Drain standing water where BLB is active. Apply copper-based bactericide/antibiotic combination on appearance of symptoms.

Rice___Bacterial_leaf_blight.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, especially late top-dressing; apply potash to improve plant tolerance as per soil test.
prevention: Grow BLB-resistant/tolerant varieties
Use disease-free, certified seed and healthy nursery
Avoid clipping of seedling tips before transplanting in endemic tracts

Rice___Sheath_blight.cause: Fungal disease caused by Rhizoctonia solani. Favoured by dense planting, high nitrogen, high humidity and warm temperatures (28-32°C); survives in soil and infected debris as sclerotia.
Rice___Sheath_blight.treatment: Avoid close spacing and excess nitrogen. Drain field periodically to reduce humidity at the base. Apply fungicide when disease appears in the lower canopy, especially in densely planted, high-nitrogen fields.

Rice___Sheath_blight.fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in split doses as per soil test; avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes dense canopy and disease spread.

Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization
Drain and dry the field intermittently to reduce basal humidity
Remove and destroy infected stubble/debris after harvest to reduce sclerotial carryover

Lesions enlarge and coalesce, causing extensive leaf blighting
Lower leaves are usually affected first and disease progresses upward
Severe infection reduces photosynthetic area and grain filling
Corn_(maize)___Turcicum_leaf_blight.cause: Fungal disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum (syn. Helminthosporium turcicum). Favoured by moderate temperature (18-27°C), high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness.

Corn_(maize)___Turcicum_leaf_blight.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; adequate potash improves tolerance to leaf blight.

Rotate with non-cereal crops to break the disease cycle

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust.cause: Fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi. Favoured by cool nights, high humidity/dew and moderate day temperatures (16-23°C).

Avoid very early sowing in regions where cool, humid weather favours rust
Ensure good field aeration through recommended spacing
Monitor regularly and act promptly on first appearance of pustules

Sorghum_(Jowar)___Grain_mold.cause: Caused by a complex of fungi (Fusarium, Curvularia, Alternaria, Phoma and others) that infect grain from flowering to maturity. Favoured by rain and high humidity during flowering to grain maturity.
Sorghum_(Jowar)___Grain_mold.treatment: Grow tolerant varieties/hybrids and time sowing so that grain maturity avoids peak rains. Harvest promptly at maturity and dry grain quickly. Spray fungicide at 50% flowering and again 10 days later in high-risk (rainy-season) crops.

Sorghum_(Jowar)___Grain_mold.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; avoid excess nitrogen close to flowering.
prevention: Grow grain mold-tolerant varieties/hybrids
Time sowing so flowering/grain maturity avoids the wettest period
Harvest at physiological maturity without delay and dry grain promptly
Avoid dense canopy; ensure good aeration around panicles

Sorghum_(Jowar)___Anthracnose.cause: Fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum sublineola (syn. C. graminicola). Survives in crop residue and seed; favoured by warm, humid weather.

White, downy fungal growth on the underside of affected leaves, especially in humid mornings

Severely affected plants are stunted and may not produce grain
Sorghum_(Jowar)___Downy_mildew.cause: Fungal disease (oomycete) caused by Peronosclerospora sorghi. Survives as oospores in soil and infected residue; spreads through wind-borne spores under cool, humid, cloudy weather.
Sorghum_(Jowar)___Downy_mildew.treatment: Use resistant hybrids and treat seed with a metalaxyl-based fungicide before sowing. Rogue out and destroy systemically infected plants early. Rotate with non-host crops.

Sorghum_(Jowar)___Downy_mildew.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; healthy, well-nourished seedlings tolerate early infection better.

Always use metalaxyl-treated seed in endemic areas
Rogue and destroy infected plants (with shredded leaves/crazy top) before spores are released
Rotate with non-cereal crops to reduce soil-borne oospore inoculum

Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Downy_mildew.cause: Fungal disease (oomycete) caused by Sclerospora graminicola. Survives as oospores in soil/residue and spreads via wind-borne spores; favoured by high humidity and moderate temperature at the seedling stage.
Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Downy_mildew.treatment: Grow downy-mildew-resistant hybrids and always use metalaxyl-treated seed. Rogue and destroy infected (green ear) plants before spores spread. Rotate fields with non-host crops.

Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Downy_mildew.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; avoid nutrient stress in the seedling stage when susceptibility is highest.

Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Ergot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Claviceps fusiformis. Infection occurs through the stigma during flowering; favoured by high humidity and cool, cloudy weather at flowering, and by asynchronous flowering (protogyny).
Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Ergot.treatment: Grow tolerant hybrids with better flowering synchrony. Avoid staggered sowing that extends the flowering window during humid weather. Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Ergot.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; avoid conditions that cause prolonged/asynchronous flowering.

Avoid sowing schedules that expose flowering to cool, humid weather
Rogue out and destroy panicles bearing sclerotia before threshing

Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Smut.cause: Fungal disease caused by Moesziomyces (Tolyposporium) penicillariae. Floral infection occurs at flowering via wind-borne spores; favoured by high humidity during the flowering period.

Pearl_Millet_(Bajra)___Smut.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test.
prevention: Grow smut-resistant/tolerant hybrids
Rogue and destroy smutted earheads before spores are released
Avoid saving seed from smut-affected fields
Practice field sanitation and crop rotation

Sugarcane___Red_rot.cause: Fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum falcatum. Spreads mainly through infected seed cane (setts); survives in soil and crop residue; favoured by warm, humid weather and waterlogging.
Sugarcane___Red_rot.treatment: Grow red-rot-resistant varieties, the single most effective control. Use disease-free seed cane from a certified nursery, treated with fungicide before planting. Avoid ratooning susceptible/infected fields; destroy severely infected clumps.

symptoms: A long, black, whip-like structure emerges from the growing point of the cane (the diagnostic 'smut whip')
The whip is covered with a thin membrane that ruptures to release black, powdery spores
Infected canes are thin, stunted and show excessive tillering (grassy shoot appearance)
Severely affected stools may produce little or no millable cane
Sugarcane___Smut.cause: Fungal disease caused by Sporisorium scitamineum (syn. Ustilago scitaminea). Spreads through infected seed cane and wind-borne spores; survives in soil; favoured by warm, dry conditions and moisture stress.
Sugarcane___Smut.treatment: Grow smut-resistant varieties, the most effective control. Use disease-free seed cane, hot-water or fungicide treated before planting. Rogue out and destroy whip-bearing canes before spores are released; avoid ratooning heavily infected fields.

pesticides.name: Carbendazim
pesticides.dosage: 1 g per litre of water (sett treatment)
pesticides.application: Sett treatment/dip before planting to reduce sett-borne smut spores.
pesticides.source: NIPHM AESA based IPM Package – Sugarcane / ICAR-Indian Institute of Sugarcane Research

Sugarcane___Smut.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; avoid moisture stress which increases smut incidence.
prevention: Grow smut-resistant varieties recommended for the region
Use certified, disease-free, treated seed cane
Rogue out and burn whip-bearing canes before spore release, covering the whip with a bag first to avoid spreading spores
Avoid ratooning severely smut-affected fields

symptoms: Gradual yellowing, drying and wilting of leaves starting from the margins, progressing inward
Internal tissue of the stalk shows a reddish discoloration, drier than red rot and without the characteristic alcoholic smell
Shoots become thin and hollow (pithy) inside, with premature drying
Wilting often appears in patches, more severe under moisture stress or waterlogging
Sugarcane___Wilt.cause: Fungal disease caused primarily by Fusarium sacchari (and associated Fusarium/Cephalosporium species), often aggravated by moisture stress, waterlogging or borer damage. Spreads through infected seed cane and soil.
Sugarcane___Wilt.treatment: Grow wilt-tolerant varieties. Use healthy, disease-free seed cane, treated before planting. Avoid moisture stress and waterlogging, both of which predispose the crop to wilt; control internal borers that create entry wounds.

Sugarcane___Wilt.fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK as per soil test; maintain even soil moisture, avoiding both drought stress and waterlogging.
prevention: Grow wilt-tolerant varieties recommended for the region
Use certified, healthy seed cane treated before planting
Maintain balanced irrigation; avoid prolonged moisture stress or waterlogging
Control stem/internal borers that create wounds allowing fungal entry
